articles.title: Whole-Brain 4D MRA With Improved Vessel Delineation Using Undersampled Multiple Overlapping Thin-Slab Radial Acquisition.
articles.abstract: Time-resolved arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based noncontrast 4D MRA enables visualization of cerebral arterial flow dynamic patterns and holds great potential for evaluating cerebrovascular disease. However, conventional ASL 4D MRA implementations using look-locker acquisitions are susceptible to progressive RF saturation during extended readouts, leading to substantial ASL signal attenuation and loss of vessel delineation in distal arteries. These limitations potentially hinder a wider clinical translation of 4D MRA, especially when assessment of whole-brain vascular anatomy and flow dynamics is needed. This study introduces a practical and reliable ASL 4D MRA technique for whole-brain or large volumetric imaging by integrating pulsed ASL with undersampled multiple overlapping thin-slab stack-of-stars (SOS) golden-angle radial acquisition. The proposed method was evaluated against conventional single-slab 4D MRA, 3D time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA), and pseudocontinuous ASL (pCASL)-based 4D MRA in terms of vessel delineation, blood flow dynamics, and image quality. Compared to the other methods, the proposed method substantially reduced RF saturation effects and preserved signal intensities in distal small arteries, resulting in significantly improved vessel continuity and contrast throughout the cerebral vasculature, as well as reliably capturing complete inflow-to-outflow arterial flow dynamics with good scan efficiency and image quality. The proposed technique enables high-quality, time-resolved whole-brain angiography, offering a promising noncontrast imaging tool for comprehensive assessment of cerebral arterial hemodynamics in clinical and research applications.

articles.title: Combined PET imaging of tumor hypoxia and proliferation in Glioblastoma using a single injection of 18F-FMISO and 18F-FLT: Association with sites of subsequent recurrence.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intra-tumoral heterogeneity, rapid proliferation, hypoxia-driven radio-resistance, and early recurrence. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI, the standard of care imaging modality for surgical and radiotherapy planning, lacks specificity for viable tumor burden, particularly in non-enhancing regions. PURPOSE: This pilot study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative dual-tracer PET using a combined dose of 18FMISO (hypoxia) and 18FLT (proliferation) improves tumor delineation and predicts subsequent local recurrence compared with MRI. METHODS: Seven patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas (5 GBM, 2 IDH-mutant astrocytomas) underwent preoperative dual-[FMISO+FLT] static PET at 180 min post-injection, and MRI. 6/7 patients underwent resection. Tumor volumes were segmented from PET, contrast-enhanced T1 (T1-Gd), and T2-FLAIR. Postoperative resection cavities were delineated, and follow-up MRI every 3 months was used to identify recurrence. PET-defined tumor volumes extending beyond resection were correlated with subsequent recurrence sites. RESULTS: Thirteen lesions were analyzed; all showed [FMISO+FLT] uptake (mean activity concentration ratio 1.6 with the cerebellar cortex used as reference region). PET-defined tumor volumes (9.2 cc) were slightly larger than T1-Gd (7.9 cc) but smaller than T2-FLAIR (28.8 cc). PET-defined volumes frequently extended beyond MRI-defined contours (mean non-overlap 6.4 cc vs T1-Gd; 1.5 cc vs. T2-FLAIR). Of six patients undergoing resection, four developed local recurrence within 3.3 months. In all cases, recurrence arose within PET-avid regions outside the resection cavity. The other two patients with complete resection of PET-defined volumes showed a relatively prolonged progression-free-survival (PFS) and including one patient with overall survival exceeding 36 months. CONCLUSIONS: Dual-[FMISO+FLT] PET is feasible, safe, and can allow delineation of biologically viable tumor subregions, in particular within the MRI T2-FLAIR volume. This approach prospectively identified sites of subsequent local recurrence and may improve surgical planning and radiotherapy dose escalation. Larger validation studies are warranted to establish dual-tracer PET as a precision imaging paradigm in GBM.

articles.title: Radiobiological dosimetry using hybrid imaging-derived spatiotemporal dose distributions for131I therapy of metastatic thyroid cancer.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop a patient-specific radiobiological dosimetry framework that incorporates tempora dose delivery and spatial heterogeneity using hybrid imaging for 131I therapy of metastatic thyroid cancer. APPROACH: Four-dimensional particle source distributions were reconstructed for eight adults from one quantitative pretherapy single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography acquisition and three serial planar images. An in-house Monte Carlo engine transported the sources through each patient's computed tomography geometry and scored absorbed dose in 1-h bins for 23 lesions. Voxelwise Lea-Catcheside repair factors and biologically effective dose (BED) were calculated from the temporal dose profiles, followed by lesion-level equivalent uniform BED (EUBED) and tumor control probability (TCP). The administered activity required to achieve 50% TCP (TCA50) was calculated under no, partial, and complete sublethal damage repair. Tumor repopulation was evaluated separately, and sensitivity analysis of the radiobiological parameters assessed their effects on TCA50. MAIN RESULTS: Predicted tumor control varied substantially across and within patients and depended on lesion-specific dose distributions and the assumed radiobiological parameters. Of the parameters varied from 0.5 to 1.5 times baseline, the linear radiosensitivity coefficient α had the greatest effect on TCA50. Median TCA50 values were 6.99, 14.38, and 15.02 GBq under no, partial, and complete repair, respectively. Small G-factors (median, 0.0133) resulted in partial-repair TCP curves and TCA50 estimates close to those under complete repair. Increasing activity amplified spatial BED heterogeneity and produced sublinear increases in EUBED, indicating that prescriptions based only on mean absorbed dose or mean BED may overestimate treatment effectiveness. Temporal TCP trajectories revealed changes in predicted control during tumor repopulation that were not captured by endpoint TCP alone. SIGNIFICANCE: The proposed framework enables patient-specific voxelwise radiobiological modeling through TCP using one quantitative SPECT/CT acquisition and serial planar imaging. It may support biologically informed activity prescription, although its model-dependent predictions require clinical validation.

articles.title: Percutaneous cryoablation of musculoskeletal tumours: the largest reported single-centre case series - outcomes, complications and subgroup analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cryoablation is an image-guided, minimally invasive treatment technique that uses extreme cold to induce tumour destruction. Its role in musculoskeletal oncology has expanded in recent years, although large clinical series remain limited. This study reports a large single-centre experience of percutaneous cryoablation for musculoskeletal tumours, including metastatic lesions, benign and cartilaginous tumours, and primary bone tumours. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a single-centre retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary musculoskeletal oncology centre. All procedures were performed by a single specialist musculoskeletal interventional radiologist with over 20 years of experience. The study included patients who underwent percutaneous cryoablation for musculoskeletal tumours between June 2021 and December 2025. Clinical response, radiological response, recurrence, and complications were assessed over a median follow-up of 3 months (mean 8.7 months; range 0-48 months). Radiological response was assessed using pre-treatment and post-treatment Hounsfield Unit (HU) measurements on CT; this is not a validated radiological scoring system and is reported as a complementary, exploratory marker alongside standard clinical response assessment. Complications were graded using the CIRSE classification system. RESULTS: A total of 48 patients underwent percutaneous cryoablation during the study period. The cohort included 26 males and 22 females, with a median age of 40 years. A good or complete response was achieved in 28 patients, representing 58% of the total cohort. A partial response was achieved in seven patients, representing 15% of the total cohort. HU reduction was observed in 45 of 48 patients, representing 94% of the cohort. The overall complication rate was 6.3%, with three complications recorded among 48 procedures. No major complications or procedure-related deaths were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Cryoablation appears to be a safe and effective minimally invasive treatment for selected musculoskeletal tumours. Most patients achieved a good, complete, or partial response, with a low complication rate. Hounsfield Unit reduction after treatment may provide a useful, though as yet non-validated, marker of radiological response. Further prospective studies with longer follow-up, standardised response criteria and validated complication grading are needed to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Discovering optimal imaging planes for visualization of the connecting fibers of the lateral fibulotalocalcaneal ligament complex using 3D MRI: a technical report.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Ankle sprains often involve injury to the lateral fibulotalocalcaneal ligament complex (LFTCL). The LFTCL consists of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL), and connecting fibers (CoFi) connecting the ATFL and CFL. Technical advancements in 3D MRI imaging enable the identification of the LFTCL and CoFi. This report aims to define the optimal imaging planes for morphology assessment of the CoFi using 3D MRI sequences. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The current report included a pilot of five MRI scans. In all patients 3D proton density MRI sequences were acquired using isotropic voxels of 0.52 mm. Selected patients had no relevant ankle pathology. The LFTCL was identified, and optimal imaging planes were assessed in axial and sagittal views, relative to the predefined neutral axis. Scan planes with the least number of slices (median) needed for complete visualization of the CoFi were defined as the optimal imaging planes. Anatomical features of the CoFi were evaluated, including signal intensity, continuity, bundle count, shape, orientation, length, and intrinsic angle. RESULTS: In all 5 patients, CoFi was present. The axial optimal plane was a 25° scan angle tilted cranially relative to the neutral axis. The sagittal optimal plane was a 0° scan angle relative to the neutral axis. The CoFi consisted of one or two bundles, which were all continuous, mostly arciform, and ventrocranially oriented. The length of the CoFi ranged from 40.5 to 45.8 mm in the axial plane. The intrinsic angle of the CoFi ranged from 124.6 to 155.0° in the sagittal plane. CONCLUSION: The optimal imaging planes identified in this report allow complete visualization of the CoFi of the LFTCL using 3D MRI techniques. Knowledge of the localization and shape of the CoFi is important in patients presenting with LFTCL injury, as it enables complete assessment of continuity. Future studies including more patients are needed to define clinical importance in patients with isolated CoFi injury and complete LFTCL injury and the role of CoFi in unsuccessful conservative and surgical treatment after LFTCL injury.

articles.title: Real-world performance and misclassification patterns of deep learning for intracranial hemorrhage detection.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the real-world diagnostic accuracy and systematic misclassification patterns of a deep learning algorithm (Hevi AI) for detecting intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) on non-contrast head computed tomography (CT) within a single-center cohort. METHODS: This retrospective, single-center study included 1,617 emergency non-contrast head CT examinations. Two expert radiologists served as the reference standard. The algorithm's binary detection performance (sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value [NPV]) and subtyping accuracy were analyzed. Statistical analyses evaluated age and sex differences between false-positive (FP) and true-negative (TN) cases. RESULTS: The reference standard ICH prevalence was 13.4% (n = 218). The algorithm demonstrated 98.17% sensitivity, 94.71% specificity and 99.70% NPV for hemorrhage detection. Specificity demonstrated an inverse relationship with patient age (96.95% in < 50 years, 93.04% in 50-70 years, and 88.54% in > 70 years). Among 74 FP cases, isolated subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) was the most frequent misclassification (62.16%). The mean age of FP cases (56.3 ± 22.3 years) was significantly higher than that of TN cases (40.5 ± 25.2 years) (p < 0.001). Subtyping errors (n = 96) predominantly showed an "over-labeling" pattern: 49 cases (51.0%) involved unnecessary epidural hemorrhage components added to subdural hemorrhages, and 31 cases (32.3%) involved unnecessary SAH additions. CONCLUSIONS: While the Hevi AI algorithm demonstrates high sensitivity and an excellent NPV that support its utility in worklist prioritization, it exhibits specific neuroanatomical blind spots. Ischemic processes, vasogenic edema, and age-related structural changes are major sources of FP alerts. Furthermore, the algorithm systematically struggles to differentiate fine extra-axial boundaries, leading to over-labeling. Recognizing these specific failure patterns and geriatric variations is essential for safe clinical integration and accurate interpretation of AI-assisted neuroimaging.

articles.title: Summary cerebral small-vessel disease score mediates white-matter microstructural and perfusion changes in mild cognitive impairment: a diffusion kurtosis imaging and arterial spin labeling study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The summary cerebral small-vessel disease (CSVD) score reflects brain-damage severity, but its relationship with white-matter (WM) integrity and cerebral perfusion remains unclear. Here, we aimed to explore how this score links WM microstructure and cerebral blood flow (CBF). METHODS: We included 31 patients with CSVD and mild cognitive impairment (CSVD-MCI) and 31 matched healthy controls. Diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) and three-dimensional arterial spin labeling were used with tract-based spatial statistics to assess group differences in axial kurtosis, mean kurtosis (MK), radial kurtosis (RK) and CBF. Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses and mediation effects analyses were performed. RESULTS: CSVD-MCI patients showed widespread WM damage and reduced CBF. In the bilateral superior corona radiata (SCR), the summary CSVD score was negatively correlated with MK, RK, and CBF, whereas MK and RK were positively correlated with CBF. Mediation analysis revealed that the summary CSVD score statistically accounted for indirect effects of CBF on MK and RK in the SCR. CONCLUSION: In CSVD-MCI, reduced CBF, higher cumulative lesion burden, and WM microstructural damage were linked in a tract-specific pattern. The summary CSVD score statistically accounted for part of the association between CBF and DKI-derived WM metrics in the SCR, supporting its role as an imaging marker that integrates vascular and structural injury.

articles.title: Diffusion-Relaxation Correlation Spectroscopic MRI in Adult Gliomas: Spectral Heterogeneity and Associations With Histomolecular Features.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preoperative MRI characterization of glioma histomolecular features is limited by intratumoral heterogeneity and the scalar nature of conventional diffusion and relaxation metrics. PURPOSE: To characterize glioma heterogeneity using diffusion-relaxation correlation spectroscopic imaging (DR-CSI) and evaluate associations with glioma grade, isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status, and Ki-67 index. STUDY TYPE: Prospective. POPULATION: Fifty Three treatment-naïve adults with histopathologically confirmed gliomas (mean age, 49.0 ± 13.9 years; 34 men). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T; multi-b, multi-TE diffusion-relaxation spin-echo echo-planar imaging sequence. ASSESSMENT: Voxelwise D-T2 spectra were reconstructed from multi-b-value, multi-echo-time data and clustered into seven spectral subregions (V1-V7). Spectral fractions and conventional metrics were normalized to normal-appearing white matter (NAWM): nV1-nV7, nADC1, and nT21 were obtained from the entire non-necrotic tumor, whereas nADC2 and nT22 were obtained from enhancing tumor (ET) in substantially enhancing lesions or non-enhancing tumor (NET) in lesions with little or no enhancement. Associations of these metrics with glioma grade (high or low), Ki-67 index, and IDH status (wild type or mutant) were investigated. STATISTICAL TESTS: Mann-Whitney U test, Spearman rank correlation coefficient (ρ), logistic regression, likelihood ratio testing, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, bootstrapped area under ROC curve (AUC). SIGNIFICANCE: p < 0.05. RESULTS: DR-CSI showed distinct D-T2 spectral patterns across ET, NET, necrosis/cystic change, and NAWM. nV3 significantly correlated with Ki-67 index (ρ = 0.401) and remained significantly associated with high-grade status after age adjustment (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] increase = 6.020). nV5 was significantly associated with IDH-mutant status after age adjustment (OR per SD increase, 10.980). Including nV3 in addition to age significantly improved grade model fit (bootstrap-corrected AUC, 0.805 vs. 0.709). Including nADC2 and nV5 in addition to age significantly improved IDH model fit over age alone (bootstrap-corrected AUC, 0.953 vs. 0.877). DATA CONCLUSION: DR-CSI characterized D-T2 compartment spectral heterogeneity in gliomas, and DR-CSI metrics were associated with grade, Ki-67 index, and IDH status. These findings support DR-CSI as a composition-sensitive MRI approach for glioma heterogeneity assessment. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Accuracy of Large Language Model Chatbots in Retrieving MRI Safety Conditions for Medical Implants.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retrieving MRI safety conditions for implanted devices is increasingly complex and time-consuming. PURPOSE: To evaluate the accuracy of internet-enabled large language model (LLM) chatbots in retrieving implant-specific MRI safety conditions, using manufacturer documentation as the reference standard. STUDY TYPE: Prospective comparative evaluation in a constructed device cohort, followed by a retrospective clinical pilot. POPULATION: Fifty purposively selected device configurations and 20 patients (10 with cardiac and 10 with noncardiac devices) referred to the MRI Safety Committee. FIELD STRENGTH: No field-strength or sequence restrictions. ASSESSMENT: Standardized single-shot prompts requested eight parameters from ChatGPT-5.0, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5: MRI safety label, field strengths, eligible regions/centering, transmit-coil restrictions, RF exposure limits, maximum spatial gradient, maximum gradient slew rate, and scan duration. Two radiologists (10 and 25 years' experience) and an MRI technologist (32 years) independently scored 1200 parameter-level outputs against manufacturer Instructions for use and technical manuals using a 5-point scale (5, fully correct; 1, substantively incorrect or fabricated); scores of 4-5 indicated accuracy. In the pilot, 160 outputs from ChatGPT-5.6, a newer version of the best-performing chatbot, were scored identically. STATISTICAL TESTS: Intraclass correlation coefficient; Gwet's first-order agreement coefficient (AC1); Friedman test; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; device-clustered bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs); two-sided significance threshold, p < 0.05. RESULTS: Mean ordinal scores were 4.76 (ChatGPT), 4.20 (Gemini), and 4.17 (Claude); ChatGPT scored significantly higher. Respective pooled parameter-level accuracies were 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89-0.98), 0.79 (0.71-0.86), and 0.78 (0.69-0.87). Pilot accuracy with ChatGPT-5.6 was 0.98 (95% CI, 0.94-1.00). DATA CONCLUSION: Internet-enabled LLM chatbots correctly retrieved up to 94% of MRI safety parameters in the constructed cohort and 98% in the clinical pilot. Errors occurred even with the best-performing chatbot, requiring direct verification against current manufacturer documentation before clinical use. EVIDENCE LEVEL: Stage 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Multi-Parametric Phase-Cycled Balanced Steady-State Free Precession Brain Tissue Characterization in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Time-efficient phase-cycled balanced steady-state free precession (pc-bSSFP) imaging is a novel microstructure- and myelin-sensitive approach for multi-parametric brain tissue characterization not yet evaluated in demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS). PURPOSE: To evaluate quantitative relaxometry metrics in white matter (WM) and gray matter (GM) of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and healthy control (HC) cohorts using a multi-parametric pc-bSSFP framework. STUDY TYPE: Prospective and retrospective, observational. POPULATION: Twenty RRMS patients (34.5 ± 5.9 years, female 15/20) and 10 HC subjects (33.4 ± 6.9 years, female 5/10). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T; T1-weighted magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo, T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, pc-bSSFP, B1 + mapping, single-shot spin-echo echo-planar-imaging diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). ASSESSMENT: R1, R2, and the bSSFP asymmetry index (AI) were compared between RRMS and HC across selected WM and GM regions of interest (ROIs). DTI-derived fiber-to-field angle, number of fiber orientations, and fractional anisotropy were used for parameter anisotropy analysis. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear mixed-effects models tested group, ROI, and group-by-ROI effects for each metric. Anisotropy differences between cohorts were assessed with two-sided t-tests. ROI and anisotropy tests employed false discovery rate correction with significance set at pcorr < 0.05. RESULTS: Significant group, ROI, and group-by-ROI effects were found for R1 (β = -0.16) and R2 (β = -2.84). The ROI effect was significant for AI while the group (p = 0.450) and group-by-ROI (p = 0.747) effects were non-significant. Age and sex covariates did not reach significance (Age: p = [0.563, 0.705, 0.591], Gender: p = [0.839, 0.822, 0.179], for [R1, R2, AI]). Fourteen of 16 ROIs showed significantly lower R1 and R2 (d = -4.25 to -0.85) in RRMS than HC. All ROIs remained non-significant for AI. R2 (pcorr ≥ 0.055) and AI (pcorr ≥ 0.108) anisotropy comparison between RRMS and HC groups did not reach significance. DATA CONCLUSION: Phase-cycled bSSFP relaxometry showed WM-predominant differences in RRMS, with additional whole-brain assessment including gray matter. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 1.

articles.title: Quantitative UTE MRI Differences in the Meniscus Following ACL Reconstruction: A Prospective Cohort Study Using 3D Ultrashort Echo Time Adiabatic T1rho and Magnetization Transfer Imaging.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: ACLR is associated with altered joint loading and increased risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Conventional MRI has limited sensitivity to early meniscal differences because of short-T2 signal decay and magic-angle effects. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether 3D ultrashort echo time imaging-based adiabatic T1rho (UTE-Adiab-T1rho) and ultrashort echo time imaging-based macromolecular fraction (UTE-MMF) identify regional quantitative MRI differences after ACLR. STUDY TYPE: Prospective longitudinal cohort study. POPULATION: 30 control scans, 19 ACLR scans at 6-12 months, and 13 ACLR scans at 12+ months were analyzed. Mean ages were 34.5, 34.5, and 37.2 years; female/male counts were 15/15, 9/10, and 8/5. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Participants underwent 3-T knee MRI with 3D fat-saturated UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE magnetization transfer sequences. ASSESSMENT: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF maps were generated with single-component exponential and two-pool magnetization transfer models. Values were extracted from four meniscal regions of interest by a blinded reader, with blinded redelineation in a subset. Patient-reported outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated observations. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction was applied. RESULTS: UTE-Adiab-T1rho showed significant group (q = 0.001) and region (q < 0.001) effects. Compared with controls, UTE-Adiab-T1rho was higher in LAM at 6-12 months (+5.60 ms; q = 0.035) and 12+ months (+7.09 ms; q = 0.028), and in LPM at 12+ months (+6.35 ms; q = 0.035). UTE-MMF showed significant group (q = 0.041) and region (q < 0.001) effects. LPM UTE-MMF was lower than controls at 6-12 months (-3.56 percentage points; q = 0.028) and 12+ months (-3.10 percentage points; q = 0.049). No 6-12 versus 12+ month MRI or PROM contrast survived FDR correction. MRI-PROM associations were not FDR-significant (all q ≥ 0.383). DATA CONCLUSION: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF mapping identified regional MRI differences after ACLR. Pairwise differences were concentrated in lateral regions, but corrected group-by-region interactions were not significant. PROMs were worse after ACLR but did not differ between postoperative windows after correction. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY STAGE: 2.

articles.title: The origin and evolution of the READ/REAL project: a national learning initiative of the Royal College of Radiologists.
articles.abstract: The Radiology Events and Learning (REAL) initiative is a national project of the Royal College of Radiologists (RCR). The RCR is an international organisation whose members are based throughout the United Kingdom and around the world. The REAL project provides a platform through which radiologists can connect, share experiences, and learn from one another at a national level by disseminating lessons from radiological errors in a psychologically safe environment, with the aim of reducing future incidents and ultimately improving patient safety. This article chronicles the development of the Radiology Events and Discrepancies (READ) project, from its initial conception in 2010-2011 through its launch by the RCR in 2012 and its subsequent evolution into READ and then REAL. It includes a brief review of the literature, outlines the RCR's work on radiological errors before the establishment of READ, and highlights key milestones in the project's development under successive chairs and panel members. In doing so, it recognises the contributions of the RCR, the READ/REAL Panel, and the many members whose cases, articles, and expertise have supported shared learning over the past decade. This project has had contributions from patients as well. This article aims to provide an index of key publications and resources available on the RCR website, serving as a signpost to facilitate members' engagement with its extensive educational and professional content. We believe that the REAL initiative by the RCR is now an established national platform for professional dialogue, fostering shared learning from errors and adverse events.

articles.title: State of the art imaging in ovarian carcinomatosis: how the radiologist can help plan management.
articles.abstract: Ovarian cancer (OC) is the leading cause of gynaecological cancer mortality and is most often diagnosed at an advanced stage due to its subtle early clinical presentation and characteristic peritoneal dissemination. High-grade serous carcinoma represents the predominant epithelial subtype and frequently presents with extensive peritoneal disease, making accurate preoperative evaluation essential. Management of advanced OC (AOC) hinges on the selection of patients for primary cytoreductive surgery vs neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval cytoreduction, with complete cytoreduction remaining the strongest prognostic factor. Radiologists therefore play a critical role in assessing disease distribution, identifying features suggestive of unresectability, and guiding multidisciplinary decision-making. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is the first-line modality for staging AOC, providing comprehensive assessment of peritoneal, nodal, and extra-abdominal disease. Despite its established utility, CT has reduced sensitivity for small-volume implants and involvement in surgically complex regions. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior soft tissue characterisation and improves detection of peritoneal disease along the bowel serosa, mesentery, and subdiaphragmatic spaces, particularly through diffusion-weighted and contrast-enhanced techniques. Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT provides complementary metabolic information that can enhance detection of nodal and extraperitoneal metastases in selected cases. Emerging quantitative techniques, including radiomics and machine learning-based analysis, have the potential to extract biologically relevant imaging biomarkers, refine predictions of resectability, and stratify recurrence risk. Integrating these tools with conventional imaging may further support personalised treatment pathways. This review summarises current evidence regarding CT, MRI, and PET in the evaluation of peritoneal disease in AOC and highlights how imaging advances and radiologist expertise can optimise surgical planning and guide management strategies.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence in acute stroke imaging: A comprehensive survey from imaging assessment to outcome prediction.
articles.abstract: Acute strokes encompass two main types: acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Each type involves specific imaging techniques and entails different clinical considerations. While deep learning has facilitated the analysis of stroke imaging autonomously, the technical differences between these two stroke types have not been examined within a shared analytical framework. This review addresses that gap through the examination of 84 peer-reviewed articles. A PRISMA-compliant search was conducted using multiple databases. Analysis of the ICH pipeline predominantly uses CT imaging and is primarily centered on a classification task. The main focus is on hemorrhage identification, subtype classification, hematoma expansion prediction, and forecasting associated clinical outcomes. The AIS pipeline is primarily based on quantification and therefore uses a variety of imaging techniques to optimize and automate the analysis of a specific set of clinical questions related to the stroke. Core tasks include segmentation of the infarct area, assessment scoring, large vessel occlusion, core-penumbra mismatch analysis, and prediction of outcomes. Convergence is also observed in outcome prediction approaches across both domains. Existing models demonstrate clinically acceptable performance across numerous tasks. Clinical deployment nonetheless remains limited by the lack of external validation, high costs of annotation, demands of real-time processing, and poor prospective evidence. This review offers practical guidance to develop fully operational AI systems that can be integrated into emergency stroke care.

articles.title: Ultrasonographic Diagnosis of Ectopic Ureter Draining into the Vagina or Vestibule.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the ultrasound diagnostic performance in female pediatric patients with ectopic-ureter insertion into the vagina/vestibule or urethra/bladder neck and to compare patient characteristics. METHODS: Of 34 patients (35 vesicoureteral junctions), ultrasonically evaluated ectopic-ureter presence and location (vagina/vestibule or urethra/bladder neck). Patients were classified into 2 groups based on surgical findings: with vagina/vestibule or urethra/bladder-neck insertion. Correct/incorrect location of ectopic-ureter insertion using ultrasound, presence/absence of nonfunctional kidneys, a duplex collecting system, and duplex vagina were compared between both groups using Fisher's exact test. RESULTS: Of 35 vesicoureteral junctions, 5 could not be evaluated at the junction, 30 (85.7%) had a suspected ectopic ureter, and 26 (74.3%) had a correct location diagnosis. Of 14 with vagina/vestibule insertion, 7 (50.0%) had correctly diagnosed locations. Of 21 with urethra/bladder-neck insertion, 19 (90.5%) were correctly diagnosed using ultrasound. Of the 13 of 15 patients with nonfunctional kidneys/duplex urinary system, 9 of 1 had findings involving the vagina/vestibule, and 4 of 14 had findings involving the urethra/bladder neck. Statistically significant differences were observed in correct/incorrect ultrasound diagnosis for the location of ectopic-ureter insertions (vagina/vestibule, 7/7; urethra/bladder-neck insertions, 19/2; p = .015), nonfunctional/functional kidneys (vagina/vestibule, 9/5; urethra/bladder-neck insertions, 4/17; p = .012), and presence/absence of duplex collecting system on the ipsilateral side of the ectopic ureter (vagina/vestibule 1/13; urethra/bladder-neck insertions, 14/7; p < .001). There were no significant differences in presence/absence of duplex vagina (p = .090). CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound was useful in detecting ectopic-ureter presence. However, the diagnostic performance for determining the location of vagina/vestibule insertions was approximately 50%. Sonographers should carefully evaluate the vesicoureteral-insertion location, particularly in cases with nonfunctional kidneys.

articles.title: Automated detection of retroperitoneal metastatic lymph nodes of testicular germ cell tumors from MR images using convolutional neural networks.
articles.abstract: AIM: The aim of the study was to investigate the hypothesis that machine learning-based methods can be trained to detect retroperitoneal lymph node metastasis of testicular germ cell tumours (TGCTs) from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) diffusion -weighted images (DWIs) and T2-weighted images. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Fifty patients were included, 46 cases of metastasis and 4 controls (mean age 33 years, range 20 to 65 years) and a retrospective analysis was done. The metastases were manually segmented from DWI- and T2-weighted images individually. Both groups were individually analysed by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to find out the capability of artificial intelligence (AI) to detect metastatic retroperitoneal lymph nodes of TGCT. RESULTS: CNNs detected retroperitoneal lymph node metastases with good accuracy on DWI and performed almost as well on T2-weighted images. In the DWI test group, sensitivity was 0.85 and specificity 0.79 compared to 0.73 and 0.97 for T2-weighted images, respectively. CNNs detected larger lesions better than small lesions, which was the most evident finding in the T2-weighted images. There was no significant difference in detection performance between seminoma and nonseminoma patients. CONCLUSION: CNN-based automated analysis supported the hypothesis of this study and demonstrated the ability to detect retroperitoneal metastases of TGCT. Further studies involving larger cohorts are warranted before clinical implementation.

articles.title: QART or SMART? Expanding quality assurance into the Safe Management, Assurance and Reporting of radiotherapy Techniques.
Reassessment of the DTI-ALPS index in focal epilepsy.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Recent evidence highlights the limited specificity of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) along perivascular spaces (ALPS) as a noninvasive glymphatic biomarker because microstructural tract degeneration and crossing-fiber geometry confound it. We aimed to reassess the interpretation of the DTI-ALPS index in people with focal epilepsy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Seventy-nine people with drug-resistant focal epilepsy (PWFE) underwent comprehensive presurgical work-up and 3-T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Etiologies included MRI-negative epilepsy, malformations of cortical development, temporal lobe epilepsy, and low-grade epilepsy-associated tumors. DTI preprocessing was conducted using QSIPrep with automated region-of-interest (ROI) placement. Linear regression models and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to assess group differences and associations with clinical variables. Twenty-five age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included for comparison. RESULTS: Seventy-nine patients (28.6 years ± 11.3 [mean ± standard deviation]; 47 men, 32 women) and 25 healthy controls (mean age, 26.7 years ± 4.2; 11 men, 14 women) were evaluated. DTI-ALPS findings were more abnormal in lesions in proximity to the ROI (p = 0.014), implicating local white matter disruption as a modifier, which was further corroborated by reduced postoperative values. No associations were identified with disease duration, sex, or normalized gray-or white matter volumes. CONCLUSION: Our results demonstrate a distance-dependent correlation of DTI-ALPS values to the seizure onset zone in focal epilepsy, whilst no significant associations to disease duration or normalized brain volumes were found. Together, these findings suggest that local disruption of fiber tracts may act as important modifiers of this measure and warrant caution in the interpretation of the DTI-ALPS index. KEY POINTS: Question Microstructural changes may significantly confound the interpretation of the DTI-ALPS index as a surrogate parameter for glymphatic system dysfunction in epilepsy. Findings No significant differences in the DTI-ALPS index were observed comparing PWFE with healthy controls; however, lesion proximity and post-operative status significantly alter the metric. Relevance statement Local white-matter disruption and microstructural architecture may significantly alter the DTI-ALPS index; therefore, caution is warranted when interpreting the index as a glymphatic biomarker in focal epilepsy.

articles.title: Sensitivity of physeal-metaphyseal tractography correlations with height velocity for fractional anisotropy threshold selection.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography of the physeal-metaphyseal complex (PMC) provides insights into skeletal maturation. Fractional anisotropy (FA) minimal and maximal thresholds of 0.15 and 1.0, respectively, are commonly used to reconstruct tracts; these values were developed for highly organized tissues and may exclude the less organized hypertrophic and transitional zones that drive growth. Whether lowering the FA thresholds better captures growth-sensitive features and correlates with annualized height velocity is unknown. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Forty-five healthy adolescents (20 boys; 12-17 years) underwent 3 T DTI of the distal femoral PMC. Deterministic tractography was performed using nine previously untested FA threshold combinations (FA_min: 0.05, 0.10, 0.15 paired with FA_max: 0.40, 0.50, 0.60) and a conventional threshold (0.15-1.0). Partial Pearson correlations between extracted metrics (tract FA, apparent diffusion coefficient [ADC], volume) and annualized height velocity were computed, controlling for Tanner stage. RESULTS: Tract ADC showed strong positive correlations with height velocity across all thresholds (r = 0.55-0.63). Tract FA showed consistent negative correlations (r = -0.38 to -0.45). Tract volume correlations were threshold-dependent: positive at lower FA_min thresholds (r = 0.33-0.37, at FA_min = 0.05) but attenuated or reversed at higher FA_min thresholds (r = -0.26, at 0.15-1.0). CONCLUSION: Tract ADC and FA are robust metrics of growth plate activity, insensitive to FA threshold selection. Tract volume associations with height velocity are threshold-dependent, with lower FA_min thresholds capturing growth-sensitive PMC tissue and lower FA_max excluding inactive PMC tissues. These findings underscore the importance of standardized tractography parameters in growth plate DTI studies. KEY POINTS: Question How can we prevent conventional DTI FA thresholds from underestimating growth-sensitive tract volumes in the pediatric PMC? Findings Lower FA thresholds accurately capture tract volume correlations with height velocity, while tract ADC and FA correlate reliably across all thresholds. Relevance statement Optimizing FA thresholds in physeal-metaphyseal-complex DTI improves microstructural imaging correlations with height velocity, ensures reproducible data in pediatric skeletal growth studies, enhances noninvasive skeletal growth monitoring in adolescents, and potentially supplements traditional bone-age radiographs.

articles.title: Preoperative prediction of HCC microvascular invasion by multimodel peritumoral diffusion MRI.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Most studies emphasize intratumoral diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) metrics, but few studies have examined whether peritumoral DWI metrics can provide added value. We aimed to evaluate three-dimensional, multiscale, multimodel DWI parameters within intratumoral and peritumoral volumes of interest for predicting microvascular invasion (MVI) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Seventy patients with HCC, including 42 with MVI, were prospectively enrolled. We calculated parameters from monoexponential, intravoxel incoherent motion, diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), stretched-exponential model (SEM), and continuous-time random-walk models within the tumor and in 3-mm (P3) and 5-mm (P5) peritumoral rims. Features showing differences on univariable analysis were further screened using logistic regression with variance inflation factor filtering to build combined models. Diagnostic performance was assessed by areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). RESULTS: Four intratumoral diffusion-coefficient-related metrics showed significant differences between groups. In the peritumoral regions, 12 parameters differed between groups, including diffusion-coefficient-related indices and heterogeneity-related metrics. Among single parameters, P3_DKI_Kapp achieved the best discrimination for MVI (AUROC = 0.713); P5_DKI_Kapp and Tumor_SEM_DDC were selected as independent imaging predictors. After integrating alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and tumor size, the combined model (Cli-IntraPeriDWI) yielded the best performance (AUROC = 0.844). SHAP analysis indicated that higher AFP, larger tumor size, higher P5_DKI_Kapp, and lower Tumor_SEM_DDC were associated with increased MVI risk. CONCLUSION: Peritumoral DWI offers multiple biomarkers and outperforms intratumoral metrics for MVI prediction. An interpretable model integrating peritumoral and intratumoral DWI with clinical factors enables accurate, noninvasive preoperative MVI risk stratification in HCC. KEY POINTS: Question Can multiscale, multimodel peritumoral DWI metrics improve preoperative prediction of MVI in HCC compared with intratumoral DWI metrics? Findings Compared with intratumoral DWI, peritumoral DWI offered more potential imaging biomarkers and superior diagnostic capability for the preoperative diagnosis of MVI in HCC. Relevance statement By integrating intratumoral and peritumoral metrics with clinical risk factors, we developed a model achieving optimal performance and transparent decision interpretability for MVI assessment, supporting preoperative prognostic evaluation and individualized treatment planning in HCC.
